title: Anathapindika's last days
hook: dying, the great giver is taught not to cling to anything, and weeps at its depth

segments.voice: Yesterday: dakkhina, Mahapajapati's robe, and your line, made by hand. Did you make one small thing for someone? Today, another great giver, near the end. Day five hundred nine.

Anathapindika's name, tradition says, means the one who gives food to the unprotected. He's the merchant who, in the tradition, bought Jeta's Grove for the Buddha by covering the ground with coins. Again and again this year, a discourse has opened in the park he gave. Now he is very ill. He sends a man to pay his respects to the Buddha, and then to Sariputta with a request: please come, out of compassion. Sariputta comes, with Ananda. He asks how Anathapindika is. And the answer is honest: the pain is getting worse, not better. Today: Anathapindika's last days.
screen: `THE ONE WHO FEEDS THE UNPROTECTED.` → `THE GIVER OF JETA'S GROVE.` → `THE PAIN IS GETTING WORSE.`

segments.voice: He describes it plainly, in the text's images: like a strong man splitting his head with a sharp sword, like a tight strap around the head, like a butcher's knife in the belly, like being held over hot coals. Sariputta doesn't offer comfort first. He offers a training. You should train like this, householder, he says. I won't cling to the eye, and my consciousness won't depend on the eye. I won't cling to the ear. The nose, the tongue, the body, the mind. I won't cling to sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches or thoughts. Not to the elements, not to the five heaps. Not to this world, and my consciousness won't depend on this world. Not to any world beyond. Not to anything seen, heard, sensed, known, sought or explored. Line after line, everything a dying person might hold. And Anathapindika weeps. Ananda asks: are you sinking, householder? No, he says. I've served the Teacher and the monks for so long, and I've never heard a talk like this. Sariputta answers that such talks are usually given to monastics, not to lay people. And before they go, Anathapindika asks for something. Let talks like this be given to lay people too. There are those with little dust in their eyes who will be lost if they never hear it. Soon after they leave, he dies. The text says he was reborn among the gods, and came back one night to Jeta's Grove, glowing, to praise it and Sariputta. The great giver's last gift was a request: share this with everyone.
screen: `PAIN LIKE A SWORD, A STRAP, COALS` · `I WON'T CLING TO THIS` · `HE WEEPS: I'VE NEVER HEARD THIS` · `LET LAY PEOPLE HEAR IT TOO` · then, large: `NOT CLINGING TO THIS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one thing. Sit and settle. Choose one small thing you're holding today: a plan, an opinion, a worry about tomorrow, a feeling about yourself. Breathing in, notice how you hold it. Breathing out, say quietly, in Sariputta's spirit: not clinging to this. You don't have to throw it away. Just loosen the grip for one breath, then another. The bell holds the time.
Upadana. Clinging, grasping: dying, the great giver Anathapindika hears Sariputta teach not clinging to anything at all, weeps at its depth, and asks that lay people hear it too. Today's word.
Your line: not clinging to this. Today, when you feel yourself gripping something, say the line once and loosen your hands. Day five hundred nine.

howItsDone: Buddhist monks and friends visit the sick and the dying to chant and to recall teachings on non-clinging; MN 143 shows Sariputta doing exactly that.

fork.setup: you're Sariputta, at the bedside of a dying friend in great pain. what do you offer, in MN 143?
options: a training in not clinging to anything: senses, world, all of it.
a reminder of all his good deeds.
fork.reveal: Sariputta teaches non-clinging, line by line, from the eye to every world. Anathapindika weeps at its depth.

original.note: Pali upadana: clinging, grasping. Sariputta teaches Anathapindika to let it go.

trapdoor: what you thought: at a deathbed, you comfort someone.
what it means: Sariputta offers a training in not clinging, and the dying man calls it the deepest talk he's ever heard.
what a scholar hears: MN 143, the Anathapindikovada Sutta, ends with Anathapindika's request that such teaching be given to householders, a striking moment in the canon's view of lay practice.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 143, Anathapindikovada Sutta (advice to Anathapindika)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the invented count 'half the discourses you've heard this year happened in the park he gave'; MN 143 has one man sent to the Buddha and then to Sariputta, not two messengers; name meaning marked 'tradition says'; 'almost with his last breath' and the unsourced deathbed-reading claim in howItsDone removed; 'literally fuel' etymology cut from the original note.
MN 143 paraphrased. Confirm the four pain similes and the full list of things not to cling to.
The purchase of Jeta's Grove by covering the ground with coins is from the Vinaya (Cullavagga VI) and later tradition; here marked 'in the tradition'.
Confirm the ending: rebirth in the Tusita heaven and the visit to Jeta's Grove as a young deva praising Sariputta.
Deathbed and pain content: handled plainly; a Keeper may wish to soften the pain similes.
